title: SQL
html:
SQL

Declarative: you describe the result, the planner decides how. Most difficulty comes from forgetting that, and from NULL.

Order of evaluation

Not the order you write it. Roughly: FROM and joins, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT.

Two consequences that explain most confusion:

  • A SELECT alias cannot be used in WHERE - the alias does not exist yet. It can be used in ORDER BY.
  • WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups. Filtering in the wrong one either changes the answer or costs performance by aggregating rows you were going to discard.

Joins

Join Keeps
INNER rows matching on both sides
LEFT all left rows; right columns NULL when unmatched
RIGHT the mirror image, and rarely clearer than rewriting as LEFT
FULL OUTER everything from both sides
CROSS every combination

The recurring error: a LEFT JOIN with a condition on the right table placed in WHERE. That discards the unmatched rows the LEFT JOIN existed to keep, silently turning it into an INNER JOIN. Conditions on the right table belong in the ON clause.

NULL

NULL means unknown, and unknown propagates. NULL = NULL is not true, it is unknown - so WHERE x = NULL matches nothing however many rows have no value. Use IS NULL.

It follows through everywhere: NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns no rows at all; COUNT(column) skips NULLs while COUNT(*) does not; SUM over all-NULL input is NULL, not zero. Most "why is this empty" mysteries are a NULL in a comparison.

Window functions

Aggregate without collapsing rows - the row and its group's summary at the same time.

The patterns that cover most needs: ROW_NUMBER for top-N per group and de-duplication; RANK and DENSE_RANK where ties matter (RANK leaves a gap after a tie, DENSE_RANK does not); LAG and LEAD for row-to-row change; SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ...) for a running total; the same SUM without ORDER BY for a group total to divide by.

The classic mistake: ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 for "second highest". It breaks the moment two rows tie at the top, returning a duplicate of the highest. Rank the values and filter on the rank instead.

Indexes and why a query is slow

An index is usually a B-tree on one or more columns, making lookups logarithmic instead of a full scan - at the cost of slowing writes and consuming space.

An index is only usable if the query lets it be. Wrapping a column in a function, or applying arithmetic to it, generally prevents a seek: WHERE YEAR(created) = 2026 scans, WHERE created >= '2026-01-01' AND created < '2027-01-01' seeks. Composite indexes are usable left to right, so an index on (a, b) helps a query filtering on a, and usually not one filtering only on b.

Read the execution plan rather than guessing. A seek on a small range is what you want; a scan of a large table usually is not.

Transactions

ACID, and the letter that bites is isolation. The anomalies, in order of severity: dirty read (uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (a row changes between reads), phantom read (new rows appear). Higher isolation prevents more of them and holds more locks, which costs concurrency and invites deadlocks.

Keep transactions short. Never hold one open across a network call or user input.

Common mistakes

  • SELECT * in application code, which breaks when a column is added and fetches data nobody uses.
  • Querying in a loop instead of one set-based statement.
  • String-concatenating SQL. Parameterise, always - this is the entire class of injection.
  • Adding indexes without measuring, and paying the write cost for nothing.
